We generate predictions for the HI 21cm signal's statistical properties at z~6-30 using second-order perturbation theory, assuming a standard cosmology. This signal prediction serves as a benchmark for the HI 21cm intensity mapping signal produced by galaxies at the same redshift. Our predictions align with previous studies but demonstrate significant discrepancies when compared to first-order perturbation theory results from the HiMINT code, particularly in terms of the bispectrum. To address these differences, we examine the impact of removing foreground noise and non-linear signal components from the HI 21cm intensity mapping data. This analysis includes the calculation of foreground removal effects on both the power and bispectrum of the HI 21cm intensity mapping data, taking into account various instrument parameters. Our findings indicate that these foreground removal effects are highly significant, particularly in areas of real-space where the data is observed, which is consistent with previous studies. Our predictions serve as a benchmark for the HI 21cm intensity mapping data that experimentalists will obtain.

Stating that two C*-algebras, denoted as A and B, are independently generated within their direct sum equals stating that the specified completely positive map from B to A in the state space is surjective. Establishing operator stability for C*-algebras depends on the existence of such a map. In the context of Schreier families, an operator version exists and is shown to be equivalent to the statement that certain Schreier families are not equivalent.

One of the primary challenges with document recommendation systems is the diminishing quality of results over time, which can be attributed to the diverse nature and varying lengths of documents, as well as users having different levels of expertise and interests. In an effort to produce more tailored and user-friendly results, researchers have turned to context-aware recommender systems. Although some techniques, like document length analysis, have been explored in this area, they often disregard users' past behavior, limiting their effectiveness. To address this issue, this paper presents a two-phase hybrid document recommendation system, which first analyzes documents and their dimensions, and then considers users' behavior in the second phase. An automatic classification method is employed in the first phase, and a weighted hybrid approach, combining similarity and relevance, is used in the second phase. The system was implemented on the Turkish Language Technology Research Platform (TURLAP) and demonstrated superior performance in terms of accuracy, recall, and F1-score.

We use finite-dimensional approximation to demonstrate that the joint distribution of random matrix ensembles converges to a specific distribution as matrices approach infinite dimension. This demonstration relies on two key components: an approximation method for finite dimensions and the derivation of a type $B$ freeness relationship among several classes of random matrices, which also includes instances of conditional freeness.

This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties expressed in temporal logic, specifically focusing on safety, liveness, and reactiveness. We propose using the signal logic TL as a framework and develop methods for detecting violations of properties as well as providing certifications for their validity. Our approach distinguishes itself by considering both instantaneous violations occurring at specific time points and gradual violations evolving over intervals. In response, we define new forms of safety, liveness, and reactiveness suited to the characteristics of signal logic, along with associated detection algorithms for each.

The decay process $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi\pi^0\eta$ is examined in detail. A key aspect involves resonant contributions from isoscalar vector mesors that couple with the $\pi^0\eta$ system, particularly those that couple to the $a_0(980)$ and $f_0(980)$ mesors, which in turn are linked by off-diagonal mixing. Although the mixing between these mesors is not experimentally constrained, it is possible to set a limit on the process by assuming the maximal value of mixing between these mesors, which is then used to place a limit on the $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi\pi^0\eta$ five sigma. This limit is relevant for experiments at LHCb and other experiments, which may help to better understand the properties of the off-diagonal mixing between these mesors, which in turn, may provide clues about the nature of the $a_0(980)$ and $f_0(980)$ as a molecular state or a dynamical system.

The GRAVITY acquisition camera utilizes four compact, precision-aligned telescopes arranged in an L-pattern to gather light for the GRAVITY interferometer on the Very Large Telescope. A novel, self-contained instrument with adjustable parameters, the GRAVITY acquisition camera employs a laser-based position verification system and a pupil-steering mechanism to ensure precise alignment of the L-pattern. A versatile software package allows the acquisition camera to perform diverse tasks including multi-target acquisitions, pi-switching, and L-pattern alignment verification. Our team has achieved remarkable results using the acquisition camera, including verifying the L-pattern accuracy of less than 50 micrometers, precisely positioning targets at the nanometer level, and achieving an alignment tolerance of less than 10 micrometers within 1000 milliseconds.

We examine the possibility of efficient approximation schemes for generalized k-center problems in maps of doubling dimension or with constant highway dimension. The generalized k-center problem involves finding the minimum radius for a set of clusters of given sizes within a space of these properties. Our study focuses on the Single-Row Generalized k-center problem, where all but one cluster are comprised of a single point, and proves a polynomial-time $O(k^3\log k)$-approximation for maps of doubling dimension and a $O(k^3\log k)$-approximation for maps of constant highway dimension.

In our paper, it's demonstrated that every entire solution of the equation $\Delta_{\eta}^{m}f-Q_1=(\Delta_{\eta}^{k}f-Q_{2})e^{P}$ exhibits hyper-order with the same degree as the polynomial $P$, and based on this result, we establish the differential difference counterpart to Bruck's conjecture. Additionally, we have successfully proved Bruck's conjecture for the specific instance where the hyper-order of $f$ is less than $\frac{1}{2}$.

This research paper explores solving polynomial linear systems in the presence of errors, with a focus on improving the degree bound for error-terms and exploring the concept of early termination. Our findings not only refine the existing degree bound but also offer a more lenient variant of Rabin-Stearns' random algorithm that can stop prematurely, ultimately leading to a nearly deterministic algorithm with a much lower, albeit exponential, running time. In addition, this study extends the original PLS problem to a more complex scenario involving systems with errors and a variable number of equations, further broadening the application of PLS.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we demonstrate that symmetry protects a unique type of correlated photon release known as bundle emission, which involves the simultaneous emission of two photons. This phenomenon occurs when the cavity field interacts with an anharmonic oscillator, specifically a Josephson junction or a two-level system exhibiting parity symmetry. We discover that parity symmetry allows for the creation of a stable, non-decaying connection between the excited state and a specific combination of the ground state and cavity excited states. This even parity-related eigenstate remains isolated from other odd parity states, including the atom or flux-free state, and thus does not participate in photons' decay processes. We discover that this bundle emission exhibits a distinct angular pattern and can be observed experimentally.

A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been derived. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and accurately matches numerical calculations to four significant figures across a broad range of temperatures and densities. It also correctly predicts the behavior as density approaches that of the liquid phase and can be combined with empirical liquid phase equations for complete three-phase thermodynamic coverage. Numerical simulations and the derived equation demonstrate strong agreement and reveal patterns in the dimensionless internal energy and coefficient of the van der Waals model, enabling reliable predictions of speed of sound and other thermodynamic properties with ease.

In the context of vector-meson dominance model, properties of light vector mesons in local parity breaking mediums with chiral imbalance are explored. By utilizing an effective action for local electromagnetic field, derived from the lowest-lying resonance contributions, spectra of light vector mesons are calculated. Research indicates that frequencies of these mesons within such mediums are shifted due to chiral imbalance and local electromagnetic fields. Notably, their asymptotic frequencies for heavy quarks, as predicted by hard thermal loop effective Lagrangian, are found to be consistent. Furthermore, it is found that the spectra of light vector mesons in such mediums, especially for lighter quarks, deviate from the quantities expected for free mesons.

We examine the task of estimating the size of a network, modeled as a graph with n nodes and a random starting point for an explorer. For each step in the exploration process, the explorer can move to an adjacent node or a newly discovered node's neighbor, with the movement determined by a probabilistic function based on the networks structure, assuming the network is undirected and connected. This model represents a small-world network, in which the distance between any two nodes is logarithmic in size, making it similar to real-world networks, such as the internet, with the assumption that most nodes are accessible within a small number of steps. This also aligns with the framework used to analyze page view counts in research on small-world networks. This problem is NP-hard under certain conditions, but when the network is noise-free, efficient algorithms can estimate the network size to a constant factor, with an expected estimation time that is suboptimal compared to current best estimates for this problem in the absence of noise. This problem is also explored in the context of Byzantine faults, where a fraction of nodes may provide incorrect information, with the goal of determining if and how this estimation task can be approximately solved under such conditions.

In numerical relativity simulations, the constraints on the initial data for Einstein's field equations can lead to numerical instability. The constraint preservation technique is essential for long-term simulations, and it is crucial for ensuring stable and accurate results. This study presents a new constraint-preserving initialization method based on the characteristic formulation. The proposed method involves solving the characteristic equations first and then deriving the metric and extrinsic curvature components, which guarantees that the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints are satisfied. Additionally, this method offers several advantages, including flexibility in choosing the boost vector and straightforward implementation. As a test case, we successfully constructed a binary black hole spaclice using this method, which shows that it preserves the constraints effectively.

The JUNO experiment, which will be situated at the Yangzhou Electron Capture detector in China, employs over 30,000 XASDICOM-compliant 20-inch PMTs produced by Hamamatsu. These PMTs underwent a comprehensive testing process at the XASDICOM experiment site, involving the analysis of anode signals and photon counts. The testing equipment used for calibration was sourced from a PIPER detector and an electromagnetic calorimeter from the PIPER project. In addition to the main testing process, the XASDICOM team also contributed to the mass testing and characterization of over 5000 PMTs for the CEPC experiment, which shares the same experimental site as the JUNO experiment.

In various real-world applications, accurately forecasting time series data is a significant challenge. Existing methods typically assume a consistent network structure and linear relationships between input and output features, which may not hold true in complex time series. This study introduces a novel framework for multi-dimensional time series prediction that overcomes these limitations by dynamically adjusting the model structure based on the time step. The framework employs two primary innovations: (1) an adaptive graph convolutional network (GCN) that creates a graph representation of the time series at each time step, and (2) an attention-based fully connected layer to unify these varying graphs for accurate forecasting. The proposed method was tested on four public datasets, and the results show that it surpasses traditional prediction methods. The adaptive GCN framework offers new possibilities for time series analysis and has the potential to guide the design of more effective deep learning models for various applications.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes are distorted by the Earth's atmosphere due to refraction, which must be corrected for to obtain accurate data. This correction is achieved by applying an atmospheric dispersion compensation (ADC) to counteract the atmospheric dispersion introduced during observations. The effectiveness of this correction is largely dependent on the accuracy of the atmospheric dispersion relation (ADR), which is influenced by the composition of the Earth's atmosphere. Despite numerous ground-based and space-based on-sky measurements of the atmosphere, there is still uncertainty surrounding the properties of atmospheric gases that produce dispersion. This project involved analyzing the atmosphere using data collected from the SALT-2 telescope, along with simulations, to determine the most accurate atmospheric models. The analysis revealed the most precise atmospheric model to date, as well as the atmospheric layers in which the majority of the atmosphere's dispersion takes place.

Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted various computer vision tasks, yet their widespread adoption is hindered by high computational costs and memory requirements. To address this issue, knowledge distillation is emerging as a promising solution, allowing smaller models to learn from multiple larger teachers. Unlike traditional distillation, which combines logits from teacher models, we propose a novel framework called Pairwise Logits Iterative Ensemble (PILE). Instead of aggregating logits from all teacher models, PILE iteratively learns pairwise logits relationships. Furthermore, it innovatively uses Student-Student pairs to enhance the overall distillation process, resulting in a substantial improvement over existing methods. Empirical evaluations on benchmark datasets confirm the superiority of our approach.

Bosonic dark matter, modeled as an ultralight wave-like field, would create minute fluctuations in the local gravitational field at its Compton wavelength, potentially amplifying faint optical or infrared signals from optical tables. These fluctuations can be detected by arranging light sources and mirrors in an interferometer and looking for Compton-induced changes in the interference pattern. A key benefit of this approach is that table-sized interferometers can be as sensitive as light wavelengths, potentially revealing the presence of very light particles. A tabletop interferometer has been built and used to set the lightest mass limit for this type of dark matter, with a minimum mass of 0.016 micro-eV per micro-eV, by leveraging the enhanced interaction range of photonic bound states in and out of the interferometer's optically trapped regions.

The basis pursuit is a widely used method for solving underdetermined linear systems, effectively bridging the gap between $l_1$-norm minimization and finding sparse solutions. Our research focuses on the relationship between the $l_1$-minimization problem and its corresponding sparse solution in the continuum. Given a fixed marginal distribution, we derive sufficient conditions for $l_1$-minimization to yield a unique solution with minimal support, which corresponds to a Bayesian maximum a posteriori estimate in certain cases. Additionally, we provide specific instances of distributions that can be modeled either in the discrete or continuum.

P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with the open-source compiler enabling users to adapt their compiled programs to various switch models and target hardware. The recently-introduced P416 language standard aims to enhance flexibility in defining complex P4 programs, with the goal of improving compile-time performance and providing more options for runtime modifications. A new compiler backend for P416-compatible programmable switches with match-action tables is presented, based on an established open-source P4 compiler with an innovative approach to compiling match-based operations. This compiler backend back-ends compile the intermediate P416 program into a switch-dependent low-level representation called P4IR, with the plan, match-action, and action operations represented as tree traversal and leaf modification operations. The compiler then compiles the P4IR program with target-dependent compiler passes, with the compiled program ultimately uploaded to the reconfigurable switch as a high-level P416 program called P4AST. Additionally, compiler statistics and a test suite of P4 programs are used to demonstrate the effectiveness of the compiler's performance, including comparison with the open-source P4 compiler.

In numerical simulations using the finite element method, Raviart-Thomas elements are commonly employed to approximate solutions to the equation du/dt + A(x) = B(x,t). However, on certain grids like quadrilaterals, approximating the transport term can pose challenges due to element constraints. A new low-order Raviart-Thomas element quadrilateral mesh discretisation method is presented in this study, preserving mass conservation while effectively capturing the solution's spatial structure. This novel approach utilizes a specific numerical flux scheme that avoids common issues while seamlessly integrating the transport equation.

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, encompassing skewed predictions and data security risks. To address these problems, experts employ fairness metrics, decentralized machine learning methods known as federated learning, or differential privacy. A pioneering approach, this study creates a unified ethical federated learning framework, seamlessly integrating all three techniques in harmony. Experimental results based on the Adult, Bank and Dutch datasets showcase the "interplay" between precision, equity, and confidentiality that occurs empirically as a direct outcome.

Scientists analyzed collision data from the LHCb experiment to identify excited states of a particular subatomic particle, known as the B-c plus. They found two peaks in the data, each corresponding to a possible state. One state has a mass of around 6841.2 MeV and fits expectations for a particular predicted state. A second state has a mass of around 6872.1 MeV and may be consistent with a different predicted state.

In the last few years, the creation of accurate numerical solutions for problems with Hamiltonian dynamics led to the establishment of a specific class of energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HBVMs). These methods can be interpreted as a continuous, multi-step approach, similar to Runge-Kutta methods but with continuous stages, and are explored here in the context of more general differential problems.

This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method that reduces the memory required for training deep neural networks. By splitting the network into two parts and assigning each part to a different processor, the framework minimizes data movement between processors and reduces the overall learning cost. When used with common activation functions like ReLU, the framework only requires a single precision sum operation to update the parameters, thus significantly lowering the cost associated with model-parallel learning. We also develop a series of techniques to further optimize the framework, including the integration of batch normalization layers across processor boundaries and reduced parameter updates. Experiments on large language models demonstrate that the proposed approach can reduce the total training cost by up to 2.5 times compared to the standard method.

We investigate the impact of dissipation on Wada basins within three-dimensional chaotic scattering. Our findings reveal that certain attractors can emerge only when a specific combination of spatial dimension and dissipation level is present. Moreover, at low levels of dissipation, the creation of additional Wada basins is facilitated and often amplified. The underlying mechanisms governing basin creation in three dimensions are explored through the analysis of unstable normal sections and repelling set structures.

A theoretical model involving an intricate scalar field, linked to a generation matrix, produces unusual but long-lasting interactions between light particles and quarks, leading to potentially observable effects in various experiments. This occurs because the coupled equations for the scalar particles, linked to various scalars, produce real roots, resulting in anomalous, long-range interactions. The model predicts a range of outcomes, including the ultra-longevity of neutrons, a non-zero electric dipole moment for the neutron, and range of boson masses, depending on the coupling constants. The range of boson masses is determined by the coupling constants, which also influence other particles, such as photons and Z bosons, in ways that can be measured experimentally.

Human action recognition in videos has far-reaching implications, but it remains a difficult task due to the large and diverse datasets required for accurate classification. This study introduces the Action-Region Network (ActionNet), a model that provides the first attempt at combining spatial and temporal attention for classifying hierarchical action categories. ActionNet employs a two-layered structure to model motion temporal relationships and classify regions, followed by a top-level attention network that aggregates feature maps to predict ultimate action categories. By outperforming current state-of-the-art models on 10 heterogeneous datasets, this study validates the proposed model and demonstrates its efficacy in action recognition.

Investigating a Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black hole with an external scalar field, a novel metric modification inspired by the shape dynamics of a naked singularity is considered. A thermal perturbation of the horizon introduces the first law of thermodynamics, and the thermodynamic behavior of the black hole is then examined. A detailed analysis of the horizon's disturbance by an infalling particle is performed to determine if the singularity can be avoided, and the validity of the weak cosmic censorship conjecture with regard to the scalar field is confirmed.

This article will examine the concept of star formation (SF) through observation, and its progression over time, offering a fresh understanding of the process, particularly relevant since planet formation emerges from it and sheds new light on the origins of life in the universe.

This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution; another with a real-world experiment involving observation scheduling for signal period estimation; and a scenario with predicting future outcomes from past data under heavy-tailed conditions.

We re-examine a wide class of nonlinear hyperbolic conservation laws, taking into account an extensive range of possible functions. Consequent to this analysis, we establish the existence of an existence weak measure-valued solution for these laws, in an appropriate space of measures, in accordance with Tarek Belaid's definition. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these solutions satisfy a certain equation of state and are unique within the given space. Our investigation also involves analyzing a specific example and its implications.

Cybersecurity is crucial and essential. Classifying attacks accurately and efficiently is a top priority. However, detecting attacks on devices with limited resources using traditional methods proves to be challenging. This research presents NBcoded, a novel encoder and naive bayes classification approach designed to identify attacks on devices with restricted resources. NBcoded is tested against the KDD CUP 99 and CIC-IDS-2017 datasets, demonstrating superiority over other models in terms of accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and AUC. Additionally, NBcoded exhibits a significantly lower training time compared to competing models.

For finitely generated infinite groups, the concept of growth rate is introduced through the examination of the expanding spheres within their respective Cayley graphs. We establish a relationship between this growth rate and the length of unique word representations in the group's generators. Specifically, we demonstrate that if a solvable group has a growth rate under a particular generating set that is not linear or quadratic, then the group contains a subgroup that is both solvable and contains a free group consisting of two generators. This implies that such group actions exhibit either linear or quadratic growth only when containing free abelian or nilpotent subgroups, respectively. We explore the growth of solvable group actions that mimic affine transformations over fields and show that these contain free abelian or nilpotent subgroups.

Animals move for various reasons such as finding food, escaping predators, or seeking suitable mates. By determining an animal's direction and speed, researchers can gain valuable insights into the direction-dependent factors like food distribution, water availability, and terrain conditions. This study presents a straightforward, high-accuracy, and low-computation method for tracking directional movement in biological entities from video footage. The approach combines direction-preserving image alignment and line-based edge detection to track movement, followed by the Robinson vector field algorithm to establish a consistent direction. When tested on a diverse dataset including fish in different environments, fruit flies in agar, and ants in a maze, the proposed method outperformed existing state-of-the-art techniques in achieving consistent and reliable movement detection, with an error margin of 10-15%.

Maximizing efficient electricity usage across transmission power networks requires optimized surplus management to minimize costs.
In our study, we demonstrated the effectiveness of using quantum annealing for optimizing power networks by defining the QUBO problem and implementing solutions on both purely quantum and hybrid architectures.
The D-Wave hybrid solver and classical solvers on Azure Quantum were utilized to solve the problem, yielding hybrid approaches that outperformed classical methods in solution quality due to lower objective function values, regardless of problem size variations.

Modern artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques are transforming our understanding of the world, particularly in the realm of uncovering hidden mathematical principles that describe how the physical world functions, beyond the scope of traditional scientific inquiry. Recent research has demonstrated that certain AI and machine learning algorithms can not only reconstruct these fundamental laws, but also detect inconsistencies between the mathematical models and observed data, guiding the progression of scientific knowledge. This insightful paper explores a range of these physics-informed and statistical AI and machine learning algorithms, accompanied by detailed case studies. It also discusses the practical applications of these models in the natural and social sciences, as well as the challenges they present.

A search for massive, enduring, positively charged particles occurring in proton-proton collisions is carried out using the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The data collected during runs 2 of the experiment at 13 TeV is examined, encompassing a vast array of possible mass and momentum loss scenarios for particles situated within the central and peripheral regions of the detector. The findings are then compared to predictions for the existence of heavy, elementary charged particles and composite models. Specifically, the study expands existing search limits for long-lived, charged particles beyond the reach of previous runs, including cases where the momentum loss of the particles decreases and they become more weakly interacting, as well as those with momentum loss of the particles decreasing. With the current findings, the maximum probability of the existence of heavy, elementary charged particles consistent with supersymmetric models and universal momentum loss is less than 1% at a 95% confidence level for particles with masses up to 80 GeV and momentum loss of the particles between 2.5 and 5 units, and the range of the particle momentum loss is expanded to 1.5 to 10 units for particles with masses of 60 GeV. We have developed a ridge waveguide structure for single-photon sources that can achieve high coupling efficiency in a low-loss integrated system. By numerically and experimentally investigating the coupling efficiency between the ridge waveguide and the plasmonic coupling section, our research demonstrates that the designed structure can produce photonic crystal fibers with a purity level of 99.6% and a high efficiency of 98.1%. This high coupling efficiency enables precise measurement of the photon statistics of the emitted light and paves the way for reliable integration into quantum information systems based on photonic crystals.

Neutron inelastic scattering is a key technique that enables the study of a broad range of vibrational modes in solids, offering insights into the dynamics of atoms. While multiple studies have focused on the boson peak, a distinctive feature observed in many glasses, the relationship between local structural characteristics and the dynamical behavior of the constituent atoms remains unclear. The purpose of this review article is to provide an in-depth examination of the past two decades of research using neutron scattering, along with complementary techniques, to investigate the nature of the boson peak in neutron-inelastic scattering. The study also discusses ongoing debates surrounding the type of motion responsible for the boson peak and its connection to the structural properties of the materials, as well as the connection between the boson peak and other unusual properties of glasses, such as two-level systems and excess heat capacity.

High-energy physics experiments at particle colliders are conducted with the goal of matching quantum field theory predictions to an unprecedented level of precision. This demands accurate calculations of complex Feynman integrals that account for the effects of multiple loops and scales. This lecture series provides an overview of modern techniques for precise calculations, focusing on two main approaches: process-specific methods applicable to any scattering process and universal techniques applicable to any process. The analysis extends beyond standard quantum field theories to also examine principles relevant to any calculation.

In complex systems like disordered media, the way light scatters changes significantly depending on the level of disorder, leading to systems that cannot be described by conventional linear theory. We developed a new set of constraints, known as sum rules, that connect the level of light transmission through such systems to specific configurations of incoming light. These configurations, called eigenchannels, are unique pathways through the system that determine how light transmits in highly disordered systems. By using a generalized version of Rayleigh's optical reciprocity principle, we derived this new set of sum rules, which can also be applied to systems that operate below the threshold of light emission. Our theoretical framework was supported by experiments that we conducted with colloidal systems.

Researchers have discovered a distant, previously overlooked spiral arm in the plane of the Milky Way by examining gas motion. The arm lies about 3-kiloparsecs away and exhibits an abundance of molecular clouds, along with some features in radio waves and visible light. The findings suggest this structure is similar in nature to other spiral arms found closer to us. It's likely a predominant feature of the galaxy's near center, primarily composed of gas. The motion of gas along the arm indicates it's moving away from the plane at high velocities, around 50 kilometers per second. The far side of the galaxy's center may contain additional spiral arms, which could help us better understand the galaxy's structure and formation.

Observing the variety in behavior among individuals who share the same genetic makeup is crucial for comprehending the evolution of life. To investigate the phenomenon of diversity among optimal solutions in multi-objective optimization, our research focuses on the influence of multiple factors. These factors include the variety in the traits of initial solutions and the variety in the characteristics of the optimization environment. To measure diversity, we employ both quantitative, non-overlap metrics, and qualitative, clustering methods. The outcomes of our experiments reveal the significant role that the variety of the environment has in producing diverse solutions, whereas the variety of the traits of the starting points has little to no impact on the outcome. Additionally, unlike in biological evolution, the variety of the traits of the starting points does not lead to the emergence of novel types of solutions, despite an increase in the number of solutions found.

The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of agents that have separate preference lists with no preference for being unpaired. A stable pairing exists if it avoids any agent preferring an available agent to their current partner. If agents have additively separable preferences, the Preferred Available Pairings problem seeks to maximize the total satisfaction of agents in a set of separate preference lists. This results in a locally optimal solution, and we investigate its distance from the global optimum. A variant of the problem with linear preferences is also explored. A related problem, the Stable Roommates problem with Ties, involves agents being indifferent between some options and being paired optimally, with the Maximum Satisfaction score determined. This is analogous to the Preferred Available Pairings problem but for stable pairings, and we also focus on this topic.

Our study delves into how different mechanisms of electron-phonon interaction affect valley behavior in two-dimensional materials, specifically exploring inter-valley scattering and valley cooling. In addition to the conventional interaction mechanism driven by short-range deformation potential, we investigate the impact of two other mechanisms: one related to the interaction with the lattice' overall polarization field and another stemming from the lattice' effect on phonon dispersion. While all three mechanisms can cause scattering between valleys and valley cooling, their magnitudes can vary significantly. Interestingly, for certain materials like the black phosphorus bilayer and the phosphorene monolayer within specific conditions, the two alternative electron-phonon coupling mechanisms demonstrate stronger influence compared to the standard one. Consequently, these materials exhibit unique valley properties and are potential candidates for valleytronic spintronclic devices.

The notion of $\varepsilon$-cloud in a Gromov-Hausdorff class is reviewed, along with the definition of $\varepsilon$-centers for the class. It is then demonstrated that the subcollection of spaces in a given Gromov-Hausdorff class that are $\varepsilon$-cloud complete forms a new, potentially smaller, class for sufficiently large $\varepsilon$. Furthermore, it is proven that any space in a given Gromov-Hausdorff class is $\varepsilon$-equivalent to a space that is both $\varepsilon$-cloud complete and possesses an $\varepsilon$-center, also for sufficiently large $\varepsilon$.

A microstrip antenna designed to operate at millimeter wavelengths features a patch design and a ground plane with a patterned ground structure. This unique configuration significantly increases the bandwidth and beamwidth while minimizing side lobes and bandwidth limitations typically associated with millimeter wave antennas. With a operating frequency range centered at 37 GHz, this wideband patch antenna demonstrates a fractional bandwidth of 20.4% and a maximum bandwidth of 7.5 GHz. It achieves an impressive maximum total efficiency of 97.5% and is well-suited for applications requiring wide beamwidths, including massive MIMO systems and software-defined radio platforms.

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using this framework, we successfully created novel surface code decoders that outperform conventional minimum-weight maximum-likelihood decoders and exhibit remarkable stability in the presence of elevated noise levels.

The ability to control and monitor systems at the quantum level is essential for developing advanced quantum technologies. This paper presents a new method for tracking level crossings using quantum jumps and demonstrates its application for enhancing the precision of measurements. The approach utilizes two interconnected Ramsakrishna-Nagata-Kimble (RNK) setups, each containing a complex network of quantum emitters coupled with optical microcavities. By using the quantum jumps generated in these systems, researchers can detect changes that occur when the detuning between the laser and the quantum systems varies. The proposed measurement method is highly sensitive in the critical region near the critical point of the quantum phase transition and the precision of its measurements exceeds traditional statistical limitations.

The PHENIX collaboration measured direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV Au$+$Au and $d$$+$Au collisions, averaging over central and forward particle momenta of $1 < p_T < 4$ GeV/$c$.  A notable decrease in hadron production was observed in Au$+$Au compared to $d$$+$Au, particularly for high-momentum hadrons, which points to significant interactions between the hadrons and the hot, dense matter created by the collision.  Furthermore, hadron production was found to be suppressed in Au$+$Au collisions despite the hadrons receiving a "blue shift" from the direction of the photon in both collisions, indicating that the suppression stems from interactions with the hadrons and the medium.  This points to the hadrons undergoing interactions with the medium and losing momentum as they traverse the collision zone.

In this research, we explore the concept of hybrid digital-analog quantum computation to simulate complex fermionic systems on quantum computers, converting fermionic interactions into interactions between excited states of qubits through a Jordan-Wigner transformation. The analog component of the simulation leverages the natural interactions of qubits, while the digital component remaps the interaction coefficients using pulsed control. The proposed approach enables constructing fermionic systems with arbitrary interaction coefficients using only P pulses, analogous to rotations of ancilla qubits in variational quantum eigensolver approaches, specifically for modeling the Fermi problem. Moreover, we demonstrate the feasibility of this hybrid approach in digital spin emulators that utilize trapped ions as analog quantum devices, and experimentally verify the accuracy of our methods by achieving 60% fidelity in preparing the ground state.

A common issue in reinforcement learning (RL) and its multi-agent version arises when two goals - optimizing performance and maintaining stability during training - conflict. Our study investigates this problem in simple grid-world scenarios with multiple agents, focusing on the differences between approaches that use learned features and those that don't. We discovered that methods that don't use learned features typically struggle to find the best solutions, whereas those that use them do not face this limitation. To overcome this problem, we developed a new framework for offline RL that creates features by combining the outcomes of several different policy models. This approach significantly reduces fluctuations in training and leads to better results, especially in grid-world scenarios involving the greatest number of agents. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this feature-based methodology and show its potential for practical applications in solving complex real-world problems in rich and noisy environments.

This study explores an advanced optical technique that utilizes a programmable light source to create complex patterns within a semi-opaque material like biological tissue. A three-dimensional complex structure can be formed inside the material by carefully controlling the flow of light, which is then detected by a sensor and adjusted through an iterative process. A closed-loop system is implemented, consisting of an adjustable light modulator, optical components, and a digital algorithm, to simultaneously create multiple complex structures, known as "vortices," at different locations and speeds of light within the material. Experimental results have demonstrated the success of this approach in forming complex structures, which are stable and have a consistent shape, when placed at various positions and speeds of light in the material. The developed system has potential for creating 3D complex structures with controlled properties and stability.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity and discuss four key points. First, DRTI generally outperforms traditional methods like regression and Q-learning in simulations, with the gap widening under greater model uncertainty. Our initial analysis utilized BTLB divergence for the specific case of binary outcomes and binary interventions, yet the method can be easily extended to other divergence measures and multi-armed bandy scenarios, with the robustness varying based on the chosen measure. The second point concerns a concern about the circular nature of the objective function. While it is acknowledged that a solution is uninformative when the training and validation data are identical, the objective function yields distinct results when these data sets are different, with the objective function balancing outcome prediction and treatment assignment. The third point concerns the issue of circular reasoning. Although the objective function can only identify one element from the treatment arm, the partial obfuscation of the ground truth outcome enables the objective function to make informed treatment choices, with the objective function modified to output partial ground truth. The fourth point concerns the objective function's ability to optimize for the target population. Our method divides the sample into multiple subsets, with each subset trained on different data, allowing the method to adapt to the target population.

Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are being tested as advanced readout technology for high-luminosity particle physics experiments. These sensors are being developed by demonstrating a prototype with interchangeable options including thin and thick epitaxial layers along with various substrate materials. In this study, a prototype was built using the thicker epitaxial layer and silicon-on-insulator substrate as previously suggested through simulation. The sensors underwent testing, analysis of breakdown voltage and energy resolution as key performance indicators. The results of the prototype are being compared to the requirements for the demonstrator to determine their suitability.

Advanced optical systems can produce exceptionally bright images, rivaling those of numerous stars, and when combined with atmospheric distortions, create a pattern of speckles. Eliminating the atmospheric effect entirely to remove the central bright spot is a long-standing aspiration in astronomy, and recent proposals suggest using coherent camera technology to control the remaining wavefront errors. This novel approach can predict and correct the atmospheric distortion in real-time, potentially removing the central speckle, and our initial laboratory results using a Fast Atmospheric Self-coherent camera prototype have confirmed its feasibility.

This study presents a novel ex-CIR model designed to address the challenge of negative interest rates by incorporating a unique feature: the model's drift, volatility, and short rate are slightly adjusted, allowing for the possibility of zero or negative values. The investigation reveals that this modification preserves the unique properties of the original model, and also provides a flexible framework for calibrating to observed market data, particularly in the light of recent negative interest rate periods. Furthermore, numerical simulations and real-world data analysis demonstrate that this model outperforms traditional affine models, such as the Fisher-Weller-Redington model, in accurately estimating skewness and producing better calendar roll yields. The model's robustness is evident in its ability to fit complex interest rate dynamics, even when volatility increases as rates decrease.

Meta-regression models are commonly used in various fields, including medical research, to analyze the relationship between research variables.  It has become standard practice to account for the heterogeneity among studies by combining both continuous and discrete predictors in these models.  Although some research suggests the use of complex modeling techniques like non-linear or multilevel models, many analysts rely on simple linear models.  However, the cluster-based variance estimator, often used after meta-regression, has rarely been tested for cases involving multiple effects within the model.  We examine the validity of these estimators in such scenarios through complex simulation models.  The study reveals that cluster-based estimators can be severely biased and lead to incorrect inferences in cases with high correlations among effects, especially when there are few studies within clusters.  The research also identifies key factors that influence the bias in these estimators, such as the correlation among effects, the distribution of cluster sizes, and the presence of unmeasured variables.  As a more reliable alternative, we propose a new class of shrinkage estimators capable of providing consistent results in such cases, and the efficacy of these estimators is further evaluated using the mean absolute deviation and the finite sample behavior of these models.

Computational fluid dynamics models that resolve individual particles can predict complex flows with high accuracy, but they struggle when simulating systems with thousands of particles undergoing frequent collisions. To overcome this limitation, we have developed an advanced integration method that separates time into multiple stages, allowing for more efficient simulations of solid-fluid interactions. By decoupling fluid flow and particle collisions on different time scales, we have been able to significantly reduce computational costs while maintaining physical accuracy. This method has been validated through simulations of particle transport and has demonstrated a substantial performance improvement, with up to an eight-fold increase in computation speed for systems with high solid volumes.

The effect of transverse momentum broadening on parton propagation through a large nucleus is examined, utilizing various models of saturation and comparing them with LHC data. These models, including IP-SAT, IP-SAT2, b-sat, b-C-sat, CGC, and IIM, are found to reproduce the data well, albeit with some discrepancies. Notably, IIM exhibits an overestimation of broadening that grows with increasing nucleus mass, whereas the other models show a more moderate trend. These results are further discussed in the context of nuclear structure functions.

This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$.

The video explores the dynamics of a liquid jet that enters a channel filled with the same fluid. As the jet interacts with the surrounding stream, it becomes encircled by a sheath of entrained air. This sheath plays a significant role in the dynamic behavior of the jet and its penetration into the stream. Additionally, we examine the instability effects that develop on the liquid jet and the consequences of these effects on its behavior in the context of fluid dynamics.

High-performance computing systems relying on volatile memory are increasingly transitioning to non-volatile memory to ensure that system crashes are recoverable. This requires implementing the algorithm-directed crash consistency model, which is achieved through the use of corresponding barriers and memory ordering, and can be automatically implemented with the aid of the checkpointer tool. This model has become a prerequisite for scientific applications in various fields, including those involving image processing, molecular dynamics, computational fluid dynamics, and computational biology. This study evaluates the performance and scalability of checkpointer on systems with and without non-volatile memory, including the use of Intel's Optane and IBM's BlueGene memory. Our results demonstrate that checkpointer incurs minimal overhead while ensuring algorithm-directed crash consistency.

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, but the automatic generation methods for these structures are limited by the need for detailed content analysis, which is impractical on a large scale. In this research, a new method is proposed for creating large-scale information hierarchies through the automatic assignment of web pages to topics, without requiring explicit content extraction. The proposed approach utilizes a modified version of the K-Means algorithm, inspired by a previous theory, for efficient and scalable document clustering. The results demonstrate that the proposed technique successfully produces large-scale topic clusters, comparable in quality to traditional content-based methods. The evaluation process involved thorough numerical analysis and the visual inspection of the generated topics, which were found to be meaningful and coherent. The experimental assessment revealed high stability in the produced clusters and significant overlap in the primary topics generated, indicating consistency across hierarchical computations. The implementation and evaluation of the method were carried out on two large datasets: the entire Wikipedia and the entire Common Crawl, which served as the basis for the experiments and showcased the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

We present a statistical prediction method for first passage time (FPT) and joint probability density function (JPDF) of three-body systems. Our approach is grounded in flux-based methods, and predictions can be made at various spatial scales, from broad to specific initial conditions. A key flux function underpins our method, and its properties are utilized to validate predictions. To verify the method, we conducted numerical experiments on three-atom Coulomb systems, comparing flux-based and energy-based approaches. Flux-based predictions outperformed others in terms of variance and JPDF accuracy, especially at lower energy levels. Furthermore, we found that the flux-based statistical prediction method remains effective even when three-body initial conditions are applied.

Measurements of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons were made in lead-lead collisions at the LHC in 2018, involving both lead-lead collisions and proton-proton collisions. The findings reveal that both prompt and nonprompt J/$\psi$ exhibits more significant suppression than $\psi$(2S), in contrast to the latter, which is suppressed less. In proton-lead collisions, all three mesons were suppressed to a similar extent, whereas in lead-lead collisions, all three mesons were suppressed to a greater extent, with the suppression increasing with collision centrality. The suppression of J/$\psi$ in lead-lead collisions was notably higher than that of $\psi$(2S), in contrast to the absence of such differences in proton-protein collisions. The study also found that the ratio of prompt J/$\psi$ to total J/$\psi$ increases with the collision's centrality, indicating a difference between these two categories under such high-energy collisions. The study found that both prompt J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons were more suppressed in lead-lead collisions than in proton-proton collisions, in terms of transverse momentum and rapidity.
